source_text: Διό περ, ἐπιδακρύσας τῷ φίλῳ, αὐτός τε τὴν κοινωνίαν τῆς ἀνθρωπείας φύσεως ἐπεδείξατο, καὶ ἡμᾶς τῶν ἐφ' ἑκάτερα ὑπερβολῶν ἠλευθέρωσε· μήτε καταμαλακίζεσθαι πρὸς τὰ πάθη, μήτε ἀναισθήτως ἔχειν τῶν λυπηρῶν ἐπιτρέπων. Ὡς οὖν κατεδέξατο τὴν πεῖναν ὁ Κύριος, τῆς στερεᾶς τροφῆς διαπνευσθείσης αὐτῷ, καὶ τὴν δίψαν προσήκατο, τῆς ὑγρότητος ἀναλωθείσης τῆς ἐν τῷ σώματι· καὶ ἐκοπίασε, τῶν μυῶν καὶ τῶν νεύρων ἐκ τῆς ὁδοιπορίας ὑπερταθέντων· οὐ τῆς θεότητος τῷ καμάτῳ δαμαζομένης, ἀλλὰ τοῦ σώ ματος τὰ ἐκ φύσεως ἐπακολουθοῦντα συμπτώματα δεχομένου οὕτω καὶ τὸ δάκρυον προσήκατο, τὸ φυ σικὸν τῇ σαρκὶ ἐπιγίνεσθαι σύμπτωμα συγχωρῶν. Ὅπερ συμβαίνει, ὅταν τὰ κοῖλα τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου, τῶν ἐκ τῆς λύπης ἀναθυμιάσεων πληρωθέντα, οἷον δι' ὀχετῶν τινων τῶν κατὰ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς πόρων τοῦ ὑγροῦ τὸ βάρος ἀποσκευάζηται. Ὅθεν ἦχοί τινες, καὶ ἴλιγγοι, καὶ σκοτώσεις ἐπὶ ταῖς ἀδοκήτοις τῶν λυπηρῶν ἀκοαῖς ἐγγίνονται, περιδονουμένης τῆς κε φαλῆς ὑπὸ τῶν ἀτμῶν, οὓς ἡ ἐπὶ τὸ βάθος τοῦ θερμοῦ συστολὴ ἀναπέμπει. Εἶτα, οἶμαι, ὥσπερ τὸ νέφος εἰς ψεκάδα, οὕτως τὸ πάχος τῶν ἀτμῶν εἰς δάκρυον διαλύεται. Ἔνθεν καὶ ἡδονή τίς ἐστι τοῖς λυπουμένοις περὶ τὸν θρῆνον, λανθανόντως διὰ τοῦ κλαίειν κενουμένου αὐτοῖς τοῦ βαρύνοντος. Συν ίστησι δὲ τοῦ λόγου τὸ ἀληθὲς ἡ πεῖρα τῶν γινομένων. Πολλοὺς γὰρ ἔγνωμεν ἐν συμφοραῖς ἀνηκέστοις ἀποστάξαι τὸ δάκρυον βιαίως ἐγκαρτερήσαντας· εἶτα τοὺς μὲν εἰς ἀνήκεστα ἐμπεσόντας πάθη, ἀποπληξίας ἢ παραλύσεις, τοὺς δὲ, καὶ παντελῶς ἀποψύξαντας, ὥσπερ ἐρείσματος ἀσθενοῦς, τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶν τῷ βάρει τῆς λύπης ὑποκλασθείσης. Ὃ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῆς φλογὸς ὁρᾷν ὑπάρχει, ὑπὸ τοῦ οἰκείου αὐτὴν καπνοῦ καταπνίγεσθαι, μὴ ὑπεξιόντος, ἀλλὰ περὶ αὐτὴν εἱλου μένου, τοῦτό φασι καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκονομούσης τὸ ζῶον δυνάμεως γίνεσθαι· ἀπομαραίνεσθαι γὰρ ὑπὸ τῶν ὀδυνηρῶν, καὶ κατασβέννυσθαι, μηδεμιᾶς γινομένης ἐπὶ τὸ ἔξω διαπνοῆς. Μὴ τοίνυν εἰς συνηγορίαν τοῦ οἰκείου πάθους τὸ τοῦ Κυρίου προβαλλέσθωσαν δάκρυον οἱ φιλόλυ ποι. Ὡς γὰρ ἡ βρῶσις, ἣν ὁ Κύριος ἔφαγεν, οὐκ ἔστιν ἡδυπαθείας ἡμῖν ἀφορμὴ, τὸ ἐναντίον μὲν οὖν, ἐγκρατείας καὶ αὐταρκείας ὅρος ὁ ἀνωτάτω· οὕτω καὶ τὸ δάκρυον οὐκ ἔστι νομοθεσία πρὸς τὸ θρηνεῖν, ἀλλὰ μέτρον εὐσχημονέστατον ἐκτεθὲν, καὶ κανὼν ἀκριβὴς, καθ' ὃν προσῆκε σεμνῶς καὶ εὐσχημόνως τοῖς τῆς φύσεως ὅροις ἐμμένοντας διαφέρειν τὰ λυπηρά. Οὔτε οὖν γυναιξὶν, οὔτε ἀνδράσιν ἐπιτέτραπται τὸ φιλοπενθὲς καὶ πολύδακρυ, ἀλλ' ὅσον ἐπιστυγνάσαι τοῖς λυπηροῖς καὶ μικρόν τι δάκρυον ἀποστάξαι, καὶ τοῦτο ἡσυχῆ, μὴ ἀναβρυχώμενον μηδὲ ὀλολύζοντα, μηδὲ καταῤῥηγνύντα χιτῶνα, ἢ κόνιν καταχεόμενον, μηδ' ἄλλο τι τοιοῦτον ἀσχημονοῦντα τῶν ἐπιτηδευομέ νων παρὰ τῶν ἀπαιδεύτως ἐχόντων πρὸς τὰ οὐράνια. Δεῖ γὰρ τὸν κεκαθαρμένον τῷ θείῳ διδασκαλίῳ, οἷον ὀχυρῷ τινι τειχίῳ τῷ ὀρθῷ λόγῳ πεφράχθαι, καὶ ἀνδρείως καὶ καρτερῶς τὰς τῶν τοιούτων παθῶν προσ βολὰς ἀπαμύνασθαι· καὶ μὴ καθάπερ εἴς τι χω ρίον ὑποκαθήμενον, τῷ ταπεινῷ καὶ ὑπείκοντι τῆς ψυχῆς, τὸν τῶν παθῶν ὄχλον ἐπιῤῥέοντα δέχεσθαι. Ἀνάνδρου γὰρ ψυχῆς, καὶ οὐδένα τόνον ἐκ τῆς ἐπὶ Θεὸν ἐλπίδος ἐχούσης, τὸ σφοδρῶς καταῤῥήγνυσθαι καὶ ὑποπίπτειν τοῖς λυπηροῖς.
orientation: Basil has just shown that Christ wept over Lazarus to support human weakness, and now explains that this weeping was a measured, natural bodily event that teaches moderation in grief.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, having wept over the friend, he himself displayed the fellowship of human nature, and freed us from the excesses on either side; neither allowing us to be softened toward the sufferings, nor to be without feeling toward the things that grieve. As therefore the Lord accepted hunger, when the solid food had been consumed within him, and admitted thirst, when the moisture in the body had been used up; and he grew weary, when the muscles and the sinews had been overstrained from the journey; not the divinity being subdued by the fatigue, but the body receiving the natural symptoms that follow; so also he admitted the tear, allowing the natural symptom to come upon the flesh. Which happens whenever the hollows of the brain, having been filled with the exhalations from grief, as through certain channels, the pores around the eyes, the weight of the moisture is discharged. Whence certain ringing sounds, and dizzy spells, and darkenings of sight come upon unexpected reports of things that grieve, the head being shaken around by the vapors, which the contraction of the heat to the depth sends up. Then, I think, just as the cloud into a drizzle, so the thickness of the vapors is dissolved into a tear. Hence there is also a certain pleasure for those who grieve in lamentation, the thing that weighs on them being emptied out unnoticed through weeping. And the experience of what happens confirms the truth of the argument. For we have known many in irremediable misfortunes who shed the tear after having endured forcefully; then some fell into irremediable sufferings, apoplexies or paralyses, and others even completely fainted away, as if of a weak prop, their strength having been broken under the weight of grief. For what one can see in the case of a flame, that it is choked by its own smoke, when it does not escape but is coiled around it, this they say also happens in the case of the power that administers the living creature; for it is withered by the pains, and extinguished, when no exhalation to the outside occurs. Therefore let not the lovers of grief put forward the Lord's tear as an advocacy for their own suffering. For just as the eating, which the Lord ate, is not an occasion for us of self-indulgence, but on the contrary, the highest standard of self-control and self-sufficiency; so also the tear is not a legislation for lamenting, but a most seemly measure set forth, and an exact rule, according to which it is fitting, remaining reverently and seemly within the boundaries of nature, to bear the things that grieve. Neither therefore to women nor to men is the love of mourning and the shedding of many tears permitted, but only so much as to be somewhat gloomy at the things that grieve and to shed a small tear, and this quietly, not bellowing nor wailing, nor tearing one's tunic, nor pouring dust over oneself, nor doing any other such unseemly thing of the practices of those who are uninstructed toward heavenly things. For it is necessary that the one who has been purified by divine teaching be fenced about, as by some strong wall, by the right word, and bravely and steadfastly ward off the assaults of such sufferings; and not, as into some low-lying and yielding place of the soul, receive the crowd of sufferings flowing in. For it belongs to an unmanly soul, and one having no tension from hope in God, to be violently broken down and to fall under the things that grieve.

choices.english: freed us from the excesses on either side
choices.why: ἠλευθέρωσε means 'freed', and the genitive with ἐφ' ἑκάτερα specifies the two opposite extremes from which liberation occurs.

choices.english: to be softened toward the sufferings
choices.why: καταμαλακίζεσθαι is passive, meaning to become soft or enervated; πρὸς with accusative indicates direction toward the sufferings.
rejected: to be weakened by the passions
to grow soft in the face of emotions

choices.why: προσίεμαι means to admit or accept something into oneself; used for thirst and the tear, it conveys willing reception of a natural bodily event.

choices.term: τὸ φυσικὸν τῇ σαρκὶ ἐπιγίνεσθαι σύμπτωμα
choices.english: the natural symptom to come upon the flesh
choices.why: σύμπτωμα is a symptom or incidental occurrence; ἐπιγίνεσθαι means to come upon or supervene, describing the tear as a natural bodily event.
rejected: the natural affection to befall the flesh
the natural occurrence to happen to the body

choices.why: φιλόλυπος is a compound of φίλος and λύπη, meaning one who loves grief; Basil uses it pejoratively for those who indulge in mourning.
μέτρον is a measure or standard; εὐσχημονέστατον is the superlative of εὐσχήμων, meaning seemly or decorous, emphasizing the propriety of Christ's tear as a norm.

pass_b_english: For this reason, when he wept over his friend, he both displayed his own sharing in human nature and freed us from the excesses on either side—not allowing us to be weakened by sufferings, nor to be without feeling in the face of griefs. So then, just as the Lord accepted hunger when the solid nourishment in him was consumed, and admitted thirst when the moisture in his body was used up, and grew weary when his muscles and sinews were stretched beyond measure by the journey—not because his divinity was subdued by the fatigue, but because his body received the symptoms that follow from nature—so also he admitted the tear, permitting the natural symptom to come upon the flesh. This happens when the hollows of the brain, filled with the exhalations from grief, discharge the weight of moisture through the passages around the eyes as through certain channels. From this come certain sounds, dizzy spells, and darkenings of sight at the unexpected reports of griefs, as the head is shaken all around by the vapors which the contraction of heat toward the depths sends upward. Then, I think, just as a cloud turns into drizzle, so the thickness of the vapors dissolves into tears. And for this reason there is a certain pleasure for those who grieve in their lament, since what weighs on them is secretly emptied out through weeping. Experience of what happens confirms the truth of this account. For we have known many who, in irremediable misfortunes, forced themselves to hold back and shed no tear; then some fell into irremediable sufferings—apoplexies or paralyses—and others died outright, their strength giving way under the weight of grief like a weak prop. For what we see happen with a flame—that it is choked by its own smoke when the smoke does not escape but swirls around it—this, they say, also happens with the power that governs the living creature: it is withered by pains and extinguished, since no exhalation to the outside occurs. Therefore let the lovers of grief not put forward the Lord's tears as an advocacy for their own suffering. For just as the food the Lord ate is not an occasion for self-indulgence for us—on the contrary, it is the highest standard of self-restraint and self-sufficiency—so also the tear is not a legislation for lamenting, but a most seemly measure set forth, and an exact rule, according to which it is fitting to bear griefs reverently and decorously while remaining within the boundaries of nature. Neither women nor men, then, are permitted love of grief and abundant tears, but only to frown somewhat at griefs and to shed a small tear—and this quietly, without bellowing or wailing, without tearing one's garment or pouring dust on oneself, or doing any other such disgraceful thing practiced by those who are uninstructed toward heavenly things. For the one purified by divine teaching must be fenced about by right reason as by a strong wall, and must bravely and steadfastly ward off the assaults of such sufferings; and not, as into some low-lying ground, receive the crowd of sufferings rushing in upon the low and yielding part of the soul. For it belongs to an unmanly soul, one that has no vigor from hope in God, to be violently torn apart and to collapse under griefs.

problems.quote: not allowing us to be softened toward the sufferings
problems.why: καταμαλακίζεσθαι means to be effeminate/softened in a bad sense, but πρὸς τὰ πάθη means 'toward sufferings' in the sense of being overcome by them, not 'toward the sufferings' as a positive orientation. The English 'softened toward' suggests compassion, but the Greek means being weakened/overcome by them.
problems.fix: not allowing us to be weakened by sufferings

problems.why: ἀποψύξαντας means they died (breathed their last), not merely 'fainted away.' The context of extreme medical consequences requires the stronger meaning.
problems.ruling: ἀποψύξαντας means 'breathed their last/died'; 'fainted away completely' misleads, losing the fatal outcome.

edits.old: not allowing us to be softened toward the sufferings
edits.new: not allowing us to be weakened by sufferings

fixed: mistranslation: 'not allowing us to be softened toward the sufferings' — καταμαλακίζεσθαι πρὸς τὰ πάθη means being weakened/overcome by sufferings, not softened toward them; edited to 'not allowing us to be weakened by sufferings'.
mistranslation: 'fainted away completely' — ἀποψύξαντας means they died (breathed their last), not merely fainted; edited to 'died outright'.

last_rejected.quote: stretched beyond measure by the journey
last_rejected.why: ὑπερταθέντων means 'overstrained/worn out,' not 'stretched beyond measure'; 'beyond measure' overstates.
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπερ- prefix = 'over, beyond'; ταθέντων = stretched; 'beyond measure' is within normal range.

last_rejected.why: Source says they forced themselves to hold back from shedding tears (ἀποστάξαι), not that they succeeded in shedding none; 'shed no tear' overstates.
last_rejected.fix: forced themselves to hold back from shedding tears
last_rejected.ruling: ἀποστάξαι τὸ δάκρυον means 'shed a tear'; with βιαίως ἐγκαρτερήσαντας, 'shed no tear' correctly conveys the result.

last_rejected.why: ἀποψύξαντας means 'breathed their last' or 'expired,' but 'died outright' misses the medical/physiological specificity; more importantly, the source says their strength was broken, causing death, not that they simply 'died outright.'
last_rejected.fix: breathed their last, their strength giving way
last_rejected.ruling: ἀποψύξαντας = 'expire/die'; 'died outright' is valid. The causal clause 'their strength giving way' is already in the English.

last_rejected.why: ἡδυπαθείας means 'luxury/soft living/pleasure-seeking,' not 'self-indulgence' broadly; but more critically, the contrast is with ἐγκρατείας καὶ αὐταρκείας—'self-indulgence' weakens the antithesis.
last_rejected.ruling: ἡδυπαθεία includes self-indulgence; contrast with ἐγκρατείας is adequately preserved.

last_rejected.why: νομοθεσία here means 'authorization' or 'license,' not 'legislation'; the tear is not a law permitting lament, but not a license/authorization for it either.
last_rejected.ruling: νομοθεσία = 'legislation'; 'not a legislation for lamenting' correctly conveys 'no law authorizing lament.'

last_rejected.why: ὅρος means 'definition/limit/standard'; but 'the highest standard' misses that it's 'the highest definition/limit'—the food defines the upper limit of self-restraint. 'Standard' alone loses the boundary sense.
last_rejected.ruling: ὅρος = 'standard/limit'; 'highest standard' is within normal range and conveys the boundary sense adequately.

last_rejected.why: ἀπαιδεύτως ἐχόντων means 'being uneducated/untaught,' but the phrase describes their disposition toward heavenly things as untrained/unformed, not merely 'uninstructed toward'; 'untrained in heavenly things' or 'unformed for heavenly things.'
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπαιδεύτως = 'uninstructed'; 'uninstructed toward heavenly things' is a valid rendering of πρὸς τὰ οὐράνια.

last_rejected.why: ὑποκαθήμενον means 'lying beneath/underlying/subject,' not 'low-lying' in topographical sense; it's a place that lies beneath, exposed to flooding, i.e., vulnerable/subject to attack.
last_rejected.ruling: ὑποκαθήμενον = 'lying beneath'; 'low-lying ground' aptly conveys vulnerability to flooding, fitting the metaphor.

last_rejected.why: τόνον means 'tone/tension/tonus,' i.e., muscular or spiritual firmness/tension; 'vigor' is too general and physical-energetic, missing the Stoic/medical sense of tensile strength.
last_rejected.ruling: τόνον = 'vigor/tension'; 'vigor' is within normal range for spiritual firmness in context.

last_rejected.why: καταῤῥήγνυσθαι means 'to be broken down/collapsed/torn asunder'; but σφοδρῶς modifies the manner, and the parallel with ὑποπίπτειν ('collapse/fall under') suggests 'broken down' or 'rent asunder' rather than 'torn apart' which suggests active violence.
last_rejected.ruling: καταῤῥήγνυσθαι = 'be torn/broken'; 'torn apart' is valid. σφοδρῶς = 'violently' is correctly rendered.
